annotation:
Line 1: M=hello; — Declares the module name as 'hello'. Every toke source file must begin with exactly one M= declaration.
Line 2: F=main():void{ — Declares a function named 'main' that takes no parameters and returns void (no value). The opening brace begins the function body.
Line 3: let msg="hello world"; — Binds the string literal "hello world" to the immutable variable 'msg'. 'let' creates an immutable binding.
Line 4: }; — Closes the function body. Function declarations end with '};'.

Line 1: M=test; — Module declaration with name 'test'.
Line 2: F=main():i64{ — Declares main returning a 64-bit signed integer.
Line 3: <42 — The '<' operator is the short-form return. Returns the integer literal 42.
Line 4: }; — Closes the function declaration.

Line 1: M=math; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=main():i64{ — Main function returning i64.
Line 3: let a=10; — Immutable binding: a is bound to 10.
Line 4: let b=20; — Immutable binding: b is bound to 20.
Line 5: let c=a+b*2; — Immutable binding: c is bound to the result of a + (b * 2). Multiplication has higher precedence than addition, so this evaluates to 10 + 40 = 50.
Line 6: <c — Returns the value of c (50).
Line 7: }; — Closes the function.

Line 1: M=calc; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=main():i64{ — Main function returning i64.
Line 3: let x=100; — Binds 100 to x.
Line 4: let y=x/4; — Binds result of integer division 100/4 = 25 to y.
Line 5: let z=y-5; — Binds 25 - 5 = 20 to z.
Line 6: <z — Returns 20.
Line 7: }; — Closes the function.

Line 1: M=funcs; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=add(a:i64;b:i64):i64{ — Declares function 'add' with two i64 parameters separated by semicolons, returning i64.
Line 3: <a+b — Returns the sum of a and b.
Line 4: }; — Closes 'add'.
Line 5: F=main():i64{ — Declares main.
Line 6: <add(3;4) — Calls add with arguments 3 and 4 (semicolon-separated). Returns the result (7).
Line 7: }; — Closes main.

Line 1: M=chain; — Module declaration.
Line 2-4: F=double(x:i64):i64{ <x*2 }; — Function that doubles its input.
Line 5-7: F=inc(x:i64):i64{ <x+1 }; — Function that increments its input by 1.
Line 8: F=main():i64{ — Main function.
Line 9: let v=double(inc(5)); — Nested function call: inc(5) returns 6, then double(6) returns 12. Result bound to v.
Line 10: <v — Returns 12.
Line 11: }; — Closes main.

Line 1: M=multi; — Module declaration.
Line 2-4: F=square — Returns n squared.
Line 5-7: F=negate — Returns 0 minus n (negation).
Line 8-13: F=abs_diff — Returns absolute difference of two values using if/el branching.
Line 14: F=main():i64{ — Main function.
Line 15: let x=square(3); — x = 9.
Line 16: let y=negate(4); — y = -4.
Line 17: <abs_diff(x;y) — Returns abs_diff(9, -4) = 13.
Line 18: }; — Closes main.

Line 1: M=branch; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=main():i64{ — Main function.
Line 3: let x=5; — Binds 5 to x.
Line 4: if(x>3){ — Evaluates the boolean expression x > 3. The condition must be of type bool.
Line 5: <1 — If true, returns 1.
Line 6: }el{ — The 'el' keyword begins the else branch, immediately following the closing brace of the if block.
Line 7: <0 — If false, returns 0.
Line 8: } — Closes the else block.
Line 9: }; — Closes the function. Since x=5 > 3, returns 1.

Line 1: M=grade; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=grade(score:i64):i64{ — Function that maps a numeric score to a grade level.
Line 3-4: if(score>89){ <4 — Score above 89 returns grade 4.
Line 5-6: }el{ if(score>79){ — Else, check if above 79.
Line 7: <3 — Score 80-89 returns grade 3.
Line 8-10: Nested else: score 70-79 returns grade 2.
Line 11: <1 — Below 70 returns grade 1.
Line 15: F=main():i64{ — Main calls grade(85), which returns 3.
Line 16: <grade(85) — Returns 3.
Line 17: }; — Closes main.

Line 1: M=loops; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=main():i64{ — Main function.
Line 3: let sum=mut.0; — Declares a mutable binding 'sum' initialized to 0. The 'mut.' prefix marks the binding as mutable, allowing reassignment.
Line 4: lp(let i=1;i<6;i=i+1){ — Loop construct with three parts separated by semicolons: init (let i=1), condition (i<6), step (i=i+1). Iterates while i < 6.
Line 5: sum=sum+i — Reassigns sum (legal because sum is mutable). Adds current i to the running total.
Line 6: }; — Closes the loop body.
Line 7: <sum — Returns the sum: 1+2+3+4+5 = 15.
Line 8: }; — Closes the function.

Line 1: M=arrsum; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=sum(arr:[i64]):i64{ — Function taking an array of i64 (written [i64]) and returning i64.
Line 3: let acc=mut.0; — Mutable accumulator initialized to 0.
Line 4: lp(let i=0;i<arr.len;i=i+1){ — Loop from 0 to arr.len (exclusive). '.len' is the built-in array length member.
Line 5: acc=acc+arr[i] — Array element access with bracket notation. Adds each element to accumulator.
Line 6: }; — Closes loop.
Line 7: <acc — Returns accumulated sum: 10+20+30 = 60.
Line 8: }; — Closes sum.
Line 9-11: Main creates array [10;20;30] (semicolon-separated elements) and returns sum(nums) = 60.

Line 1: M=arrays; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=get(arr:[i64];i:i64):i64{ — Function taking an i64 array and an index, returning the element at that index.
Line 3: <arr[i] — Array indexing with bracket notation. Returns the element at position i.
Line 4: }; — Closes get.
Line 5: F=main():i64{ — Main function.
Line 6: let a=[10;20;30;40;50]; — Array literal with 5 elements, separated by semicolons.
Line 7: let first=a[0]; — Accesses first element (10).
Line 8: let last=a[4]; — Accesses last element (50).
Line 9: <first+last — Returns 10 + 50 = 60.
Line 10: }; — Closes main.

Line 1: M=structs; — Module declaration.
Line 2: T=Point{x:i64;y:i64}; — Type declaration defining a struct 'Point' with two i64 fields: x and y. Type names must start with an uppercase letter.
Line 3: F=main():i64{ — Main function.
Line 4: let p=Point{x:3;y:4}; — Creates a struct literal of type Point with x=3 and y=4. Field initializers are separated by semicolons.
Line 5: <p.x+p.y — Dot notation accesses struct fields. Returns 3 + 4 = 7.
Line 6: }; — Closes main.

Line 1: M=vec; — Module declaration.
Line 2: T=Vec2{x:i64;y:i64}; — Struct type with x and y fields.
Line 3: F=add(a:Vec2;b:Vec2):Vec2{ — Function taking two Vec2 structs and returning a Vec2.
Line 4: <Vec2{x:a.x+b.x;y:a.y+b.y} — Constructs a new Vec2 by adding corresponding fields of a and b.
Line 5: }; — Closes add.
Line 6: F=main():i64{ — Main function.
Line 7-8: Creates two Vec2 values: a=(3,4) and b=(10,20).
Line 9: let c=add(a;b); — Calls add, producing Vec2{x:13;y:24}.
Line 10: <c.x+c.y — Returns 13 + 24 = 37.
Line 11: }; — Closes main.

Line 1: M=strings; — Module declaration.
Line 2: I=str:std.str; — Import declaration: imports the std.str module and binds it to the local alias 'str'. The I= keyword declares imports.
Line 3: F=main():i64{ — Main function.
Line 4: let a="hello"; — String literal binding.
Line 5: let b=" world"; — Another string literal.
Line 6: let c=str.concat(a;b); — Calls str.concat to concatenate the two strings, producing "hello world".
Line 7: let n=str.len(c); — Calls str.len to get the length of the concatenated string (11).
Line 8: <n — Returns 11.
Line 9: }; — Closes main.

Line 1: M=logic; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=both(a:bool;b:bool):bool{ — Function taking two booleans, returns bool. Implements logical AND.
Line 3-4: if(a){ if(b){ — Nested conditionals: checks a, then b.
Line 5: <true — Both are true, return true.
Line 6-7: }el{ <false } — b is false, return false.
Line 8-10: }el{ <false } — a is false, return false.
Line 11: }; — Closes both.
Line 12: F=main():i64{ — Main function.
Line 13: if(both(true;true)){ — Calls both with true and true. 'true' and 'false' are predefined boolean identifiers.
Line 14: <1 — Returns 1 when both are true.
Line 15-16: }el{ <0 } — Returns 0 otherwise.
Line 17: }; — Closes main.

Line 1: M=nested; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=main():i64{ — Main function.
Line 3: let a=3; — Binds 3 to a.
Line 4: let b=7; — Binds 7 to b.
Line 5: let c=a*b+a-b; — Evaluates with standard precedence: (3*7)+3-7 = 21+3-7 = 17.
Line 6: let d=c*2+a; — (17*2)+3 = 37.
Line 7: let e=d-c+b*a; — 37-17+(7*3) = 37-17+21 = 41.
Line 8: <e — Returns 41.
Line 9: }; — Closes main.

Line 1: M=deep; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=double(x:i64):i64{<x*2}; — Single-line function that doubles its input. The body can be on one line.
Line 3: F=inc(x:i64):i64{<x+1}; — Single-line function that increments by 1.
Line 4: F=main():i64{ — Main function.
Line 5: <double(double(double(inc(inc(inc(0)))))) — Deeply nested calls: inc(0)=1, inc(1)=2, inc(2)=3, double(3)=6, double(6)=12, double(12)=24. Returns 24.
Line 6: }; — Closes main.

Line 1: M=api.user; — Module declaration with a dotted path. Module paths use dots to create a hierarchical namespace.
Line 2: I=db:std.db; — Imports the std.db module, aliased locally as 'db'. After this, db.one, db.exec etc. are accessible.
Line 3: I=json:std.json; — Imports std.json, aliased as 'json'. After this, json.enc, json.dec etc. are accessible.
Line 4: T=User{id:i64;name:Str}; — Struct type declaration for User with an integer id and a Str name.
Line 5: F=create(name:Str):i64{ — Function declaration. All imports must precede type declarations, which must precede function declarations.
Line 6: <1 — Placeholder return.
Line 7: }; — Closes the function.

Line 1: M=errs; — Module declaration.
Line 2-5: T=FetchErr{ NotFound:i64; Timeout:Str }; — Sum type (tagged union) declaration. Variant names start with uppercase. NotFound carries an i64 payload, Timeout carries a Str.
Line 6: F=fetch(id:i64):Str!FetchErr{ — Function returning Str on success or FetchErr on failure. The '!' separates the success type from the error type.
Line 7-8: if(id<0){ <FetchErr.NotFound(id) — Returns an error variant when id is negative.
Line 9-10: }el{ <"found" } — Returns the success value otherwise.
Line 11: }; — Closes fetch.
Line 12-14: Main function returns 0 (placeholder).

Line 1: M=matching; — Module declaration.
Line 2-5: T=Shape{ Circle:i64; Square:i64 }; — Sum type with two variants: Circle (radius) and Square (side length).
Line 6: F=area(s:Shape):i64{ — Function taking a Shape and returning its area as i64.
Line 7: <s|{ — Match expression: the '|{' operator pattern-matches on the sum type value s.
Line 8: Circle:r r*r*3; — First match arm: if s is Circle, bind the payload to 'r', evaluate r*r*3 (approximate area).
Line 9: Square:side side*side — Second match arm: if s is Square, bind payload to 'side', evaluate side*side.
Line 10: } — Closes the match. Match must be exhaustive (cover all variants).
Line 11: }; — Closes area.
Line 12: F=main():i64{ — Main function.
Line 13: let c=Shape.Circle(5); — Constructs a Circle variant with radius 5.
Line 14: <area(c) — Returns area of circle: 5*5*3 = 75.
Line 15: }; — Closes main.

Line 1: M=mutable; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=main():i64{ — Main function.
Line 3: let x=mut.1; — Declares a mutable binding x initialized to 1. The 'mut.' prefix after '=' marks the binding as mutable.
Line 4: x=x+10; — Reassigns x to 1+10 = 11. This is legal because x was declared with mut.
Line 5: x=x*2; — Reassigns x to 11*2 = 22.
Line 6: <x — Returns 22.
Line 7: }; — Closes main.

Line 1: M=casting; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=main():i64{ — Main function.
Line 3: let narrow=42; — Binds 42 to narrow.
Line 4: let wide=narrow as i64; — The 'as' keyword performs an explicit type cast. toke has no implicit coercions; all type conversions must use 'as'.
Line 5: <wide — Returns the cast value (42).
Line 6: }; — Closes main.

Line 1: M=breaking; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=find_first_gt(arr:[i64];threshold:i64):i64{ — Function that finds the first array element greater than a threshold.
Line 3: let result=mut.0-1; — Mutable binding initialized to -1 (0-1) as a sentinel for 'not found'.
Line 4: lp(let i=0;i<arr.len;i=i+1){ — Loop iterating over array indices.
Line 5: if(arr[i]>threshold){ — Check if current element exceeds threshold.
Line 6: result=arr[i]; — Store the found element.
Line 7: br — The 'br' keyword breaks out of the innermost loop immediately.
Line 8-10: }el{ result=result } — Else branch (no-op, keeps result unchanged).
Line 11: }; — Closes loop.
Line 12: <result — Returns the first element > threshold, or -1 if none found.
Line 13: }; — Closes function.
Line 14-16: Main creates [3;7;2;9;1] and calls find_first_gt with threshold 5. First element > 5 is 7.

Line 1: M=returns; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=classify(n:i64):i64{ — Function that classifies a number as positive (1), negative (-1), or zero (0).
Line 3-4: if(n>0){ <1 — First return path: positive numbers return 1.
Line 5-7: }el{ if(n<0){ <0-1 — Second return path: negative numbers return -1 (expressed as 0-1 since toke uses '-' as binary operator).
Line 8-9: }el{ <0 } — Third return path: zero returns 0.
Line 10-11: }} — Closes nested if/el blocks.
Line 12: }; — Closes classify.
Line 13-16: Main calls classify three times: classify(5)=1, classify(-3)=-1, classify(0)=0. Returns 1+(-1)+0 = 0.

Line 1: M=arrop; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=max(arr:[i64]):i64{ — Function that finds the maximum element in an i64 array.
Line 3: let m=mut.arr[0]; — Mutable binding initialized to the first element of the array.
Line 4: lp(let i=1;i<arr.len;i=i+1){ — Loop starting from index 1 (already have index 0).
Line 5-6: if(arr[i]>m){ m=arr[i] — If current element is larger than m, update m.
Line 7-8: }el{ m=m } — Else keep m unchanged.
Line 9: }; — Closes loop.
Line 10: <m — Returns the maximum value found.
Line 11: }; — Closes max.
Line 12-14: Main creates array [4;9;2;7;1;8] and returns max = 9.

Line 1: M=recurse; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=factorial(n:i64):i64{ — Recursive function computing n factorial.
Line 3-4: if(n<2){ <1 — Base case: if n < 2, return 1.
Line 5-6: }el{ <n*factorial(n-1) } — Recursive case: return n * factorial(n-1). toke supports recursive function calls.
Line 7: }; — Closes factorial.
Line 8: F=main():i64{ — Main function.
Line 9: <factorial(5) — Computes 5! = 120.
Line 10: }; — Closes main.

Line 1: M=fib; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=fib(n:i64):i64{ — Recursive Fibonacci function.
Line 3-4: if(n<2){ <n — Base cases: fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1.
Line 5-6: }el{ <fib(n-1)+fib(n-2) } — Recursive case: sum of two preceding Fibonacci numbers. Demonstrates multiple recursive calls in a single expression.
Line 7: }; — Closes fib.
Line 8: F=main():i64{ — Main function.
Line 9: <fib(10) — Computes the 10th Fibonacci number = 55.
Line 10: }; — Closes main.

Line 1: M=voids; — Module declaration.
Line 2: F=greet():void{ — Function returning void (no value). Used for side effects.
Line 3: let x=42; — A local binding inside the void function.
Line 4: }; — Closes greet. No return statement needed for void functions.
Line 5: F=main():i64{ — Main function.
Line 6: greet(); — Calls greet as a statement. Void function calls stand alone as expression statements.
Line 7: <0 — Returns 0.
Line 8: }; — Closes main.

Line 1: M=stats; — Module declaration.
Line 2: T=Stats{min:i64;max:i64;sum:i64}; — Struct type with three fields for statistical results.
Line 3: F=compute(arr:[i64]):Stats{ — Function taking an array and returning a Stats struct.
Line 4-6: Three mutable bindings initialized to the first array element: min, max, and sum trackers.
Line 7: lp(let i=1;i<arr.len;i=i+1){ — Loop from index 1 through the array.
Line 8-12: if(arr[i]<mn){ mn=arr[i] }el{ mn=mn }; — Update minimum if current element is smaller.
Line 13-17: if(arr[i]>mx){ mx=arr[i] }el{ mx=mx }; — Update maximum if current element is larger.
Line 18: sm=sm+arr[i] — Accumulate sum.
Line 19: }; — Closes loop.
Line 20: <Stats{min:mn;max:mx;sum:sm} — Returns a Stats struct literal with computed values.
Line 21: }; — Closes compute.
Line 22-25: Main creates [5;1;8;3;9;2], computes stats, and returns the sum (5+1+8+3+9+2 = 28).
